title: Event-sourced Observability: Correlation & Triage Runbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:
This runbook defines the event-sourced observability model we use to correlate distributed runtime signals (traces, metrics, logs, kernel events) and perform fast, reproducible triage of inference incidents. It documents the canonical event envelope, enrichment rules, minimal required fields, triage playflow, example queries, and rollout checklist for instrumenting new runtime components.

Goals:
- Provide a single cross-team contract for events produced by runtime components (dispatcher, kernel, kvcache, allocator, model-swaps).
- Reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) for performance regressions and correctness incidents by standardizing correlation keys and triage steps.
- Ensure low-cost, high-utility telemetry: bounding event size, pre-aggregation guidelines, and sampling rules.

Scope and when to use:
- Use this runbook for any incident that involves latency spikes, tail latency regressions, memory pressure OOMs, soft degradation, or model swap oscillations.
- Not intended for application-layer logic bugs (customer prompt-level bugs) unless they cause runtime-level resource anomalies.

Event model (canonical envelope):
Every runtime event MUST be an immutable envelope with the following fields (minimum set):
- event_id: globally unique id (uuid4)
- ts_iso: ISO8601 timestamp in UTC
- origin_service: short name (e.g., dispatcher, kernel, kvcache, allocator)
- host_id: node identifier (k8s node / instance id)
- shard_id: runtime shard or device id when applicable (e.g., gpu-0)
- request_id: upstream request trace id if present, otherwise generated
- route_tag: customer or route identifier (when applicable)
- phase: high-level phase (ingest, scheduling, dispatch, kernel_exec, postprocessing)
- level: INFO/WARN/ERROR
- payload: structured JSON blob with event-specific fields (see examples)

Minimal telemetry fields table (copyable):
| field       | type   | example                        | notes |
|-------------|--------|--------------------------------|-------|
| event_id    | string | 9f8b6aab-...                   | uuid4 |
| ts_iso      | string | 2026-02-14T18:03:23.123Z       | UTC |
| origin_service | string | kernel                      | short service name |
| host_id     | string | i-0a1b2c3d4e5f                 | k8s node id or instance |
| shard_id    | string | gpu-0                         | device/shard context |
| request_id  | string | req-4b123                      | correlates to client request |
| route_tag   | string | prod-chat-1                   | optional but highly recommended |
| phase       | string | kernel_exec                   | one of the canonical phases |
| level       | string | WARN                          | log level |
| payload     | object | {"lat_ms": 4.2}              | event-specific details |

Event envelope example (JSON):
{
  "event_id": "9f8b6aab-1234-4cde-8a7b-0abcde123456",
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-14T18:03:23.123Z",
  "origin_service": "kernel",
  "host_id": "node-42",
  "shard_id": "gpu-0",
  "request_id": "req-4b123",
  "route_tag": "prod-chat-1",
  "phase": "kernel_exec",
  "level": "INFO",
  "payload": {
    "lat_ms": 12.4,
    "seq_len": 256,
    "kv_hit": true,
    "kernel_variant": "vectored-tc"
  }
}

Enrichment rules (construction time):
1) Attach stable host_id and shard_id at process startup. Fail open: if shard unknown, set "shard_id": "unknown".
2) Propagate request_id from surface API through the dispatcher to the kernel; if absent, synthesize and mark with a "synthesized_request_id" boolean in payload.
3) Route tagging: upstream routers should add route_tag; if missing, call-site should derive route from model_id or team config.
4) Add deployment metadata (commit hash, kernel build id) to host-level heartbeat events produced every 5 minutes.

Sampling and retention guidance:
- Full tracing is expensive. Apply progressive sampling: 100% sampling for ERROR events, 10% for WARN, and reservoir sampling for INFO subject to label-based overrides (e.g., always sample requests tagged as "perf-eval").
- For high-volume kernels, emit aggregated rollup events per minute per shard with the fields: ts_minute, shard_id, kernel_variant, q1,q50,q95,q99,invocations,total_tokens. Use these for fast dashboards and cost-aware alerts.

Triage playflow (step-by-step):
1) Detect: alert triggers (e.g., p99 latency > SLO threshold on a route) should create an incident ticket with a link to the minute rollup and sample traces.
2) Initial burst analysis (5 min): run the minute rollup query filtered by route_tag -> check p50/p95/p99 delta, invocation count, token distribution.
3) Correlate with host-level signals: filter events by ts range and examine host heartbeats for thermal/power anomalies, collector reports for kernel build mismatch, and allocator warnings.
4) Expand to kernel-level events: pull kernel_exec events for the suspect shards and examine payload fields (lat_ms, seq_len, kernel_variant, tensor_core_util). Look for step changes in kernel_variant mix or sudden rise in seq_len.
5) Cross-check kvcache: look for kvcache miss spikes in the same time window using payload.kv_hit==false and kvcache warmup events. A kvcache miss storm often explains latency spikes.
6) If no kernel resource anomaly, inspect dispatcher and admission controller events for queue depth, preemption, or credit exhaustion.
7) If root cause unclear, collect a deterministic trace sample: set temporary sampling override to 100% for the offending route_tag for 2 minutes and capture full traces.
8) Containment: based on root cause, apply one of the quick mitigations (see Quick mitigations below), open a rollback or canary pause if needed, and annotate incident ticket with event ids of representative traces.

Quick mitigations (common):
- Increase per-route concurrency cap by +20% for 2 min via routing console (when admission controller is too restrictive).
- Temporarily pin route to a lower-fidelity model-variant to avoid kernel stalls.
- Evict cold kvcache on a small percentage of nodes to re-balance warm cache.
- Throttle low-priority background workloads on nodes reporting thermal or memory pressure.

Example KQL/SQL queries (schematic):
1) Minute rollup for route: SELECT ts_minute, shard_id, kernel_variant, q50, q95, q99, invocations FROM runtime_rollups WHERE route_tag = 'prod-chat-1' AND ts_minute BETWEEN x AND y ORDER BY ts_minute;
2) Kernel event histogram: SELECT bucket(lat_ms, [0,1,2,5,10,20,50,100]) AS lat_bkt, count(*) FROM events WHERE origin_service='kernel' AND ts_iso BETWEEN ... GROUP BY lat_bkt;
3) Correlate kvcache misses: SELECT request_id, ts_iso, payload.kv_hit, payload.seq_len FROM events WHERE origin_service IN ('kvcache','kernel') AND ts_iso BETWEEN ... AND route_tag='prod-chat-1' ORDER BY ts_iso LIMIT 500;

Investigation checklist (runnable):
- Reproduce local microbench with same kernel_variant and seq_len distribution.
- Compare kernel build id from host heartbeat to the canary fleet build id.
- Run a synthetic traffic replay using the request surface replay harness with identical token distribution.
- If memory pressure suspected, capture allocator diagnostic snapshot (see allocator-runbook).

Runbook for kernel regression rollback decision: (decision matrix)
- Severity: P0 (customer impacting or SLO breach > 1 hour): immediate rollback to last known good kernel_variant and schedule hotfix release.
- Severity: P1 (intermittent SLO breach < 1 hour): throttle traffic via routing and open detailed profiling ticket.
- Severity: P2: schedule follow-up experiment and kernel bisect.

Ownership, SLAs and notifications:
- Primary owner for this contract: Serving Runtime Observability (oncall): runtime-observability@redwood.ai.
- Oncall response SLA: acknowledge within 15 minutes for P0/P1, start triage within 30 minutes.
- Postmortem requirement: detailed incident postmortem for any event that caused > 1 hour SLO breach or > 5% customer error increase.

Rollout checklist for instrumenting a new component into the contract:
1) Add the canonical envelope producer to the component library with local validation.
2) Emit host-level heartbeat and attach deployment metadata.
3) Unit test event envelope, including synthesized request_id path.
4) Stage sampling rules and verify ingestion at low volume to the ingest cluster.
5) Add dashboard tiles: per-minute rollup, p95/p99 heatmap, kvcache-hit-rate, kernel_variant mix.
6) Run a 48-hour shadow run with sample-rate parity and measure telemetry cost.

Debugging utilities and commands (examples):
- Collect live kernel traces: rtr-collect --shard gpu-0 --since 2026-02-14T18:00Z --limit 200 --output /tmp/traces.ndjson
- Query rollups: rtql "SELECT * FROM runtime_rollups WHERE route_tag='prod-chat-1' AND ts_minute >= '2026-02-14T17:00'"

Appendix: Known anti-patterns and gotchas:
- Relying solely on p95 can hide p99 regressions that are caused by rare long sequences; always check p99 and the seq_len distribution.
- Missing request_id propagation from the gateway makes correlation much slower; instrument synthetic propagation in test harnesses.
- Overly aggressive INFO sampling can starve postmortem investigators of the causal chain.
